subject: BB047A0483F7446F98969E0BB0A9A2A0
introduction: “It is not sufficient only to distinguish the way of the Kingdom … you must travel upon it until the end is reached.” The guide gathers what ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Bahá’u’lláh said about effort: that faculties are given to be used, that capacity grows by striving, that every gift but one is won by endeavour, and that the one, guidance, is bestowed; then page after page of urging, with oil left in the lamp and time a cutting sword. Proverbs sends the sluggard to the ant, Paul runs for a prize and presses toward the mark, the Qur’an promises guidance to those who strive, the Buddha says you yourself must make the effort, and Aesop, Tennyson, Longfellow and Roosevelt give the modern West its proverbs for the same thing. The other side of the ledger is long too. “It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth”; the race is not to the swift; God gives his beloved sleep; Mary sat still and chose the better part; Milton found that they also serve who only stand and wait; Augustine asked God to give what He commands; and the father of the prodigal ran.
questions: Reading 7 says every gift is attained by effort except guidance. With “it is not of him that willeth” and “work out your own salvation … for it is God which worketh in you” in view, how do the readings relate effort to grace?
The Preacher says the race is not to the swift; reading 13 says the worker in this Cause always succeeds. What kind of success can be promised without contradicting him?
“They also serve who only stand and wait”, and “he giveth his beloved sleep”. How might the many calls to ceaseless activity be read by someone ill, old or exhausted?
The fountain does not run after the thirsty, says reading 40; the father of the prodigal runs. Which readings elsewhere in the guide sound more like the father?
Herrick and reading 68 both say that time is short. What difference does it make what one hurries toward?
Reading 89 ends the guide by turning effort outward. How does that last sentence change the meaning of the striving that came before it?

outside.why: Senses and faculties are given “to be devoted to the service of the general good”. The master of the parable gives each servant talents according to his ability, and returns to ask what was done with them.
Marcus Aurelius to himself at dawn: I am rising to the work of a human being; why then am I dissatisfied, if I am going to do the things for which I exist?
To discover the way is not to travel it. James: faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
The example is a journey to America. Lao-tzu’s is any journey: a journey of a thousand li begins with a single step.
“Strive in your work but trust in God.” The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the Lord.
Poor Richard’s version, “God helps them that help themselves”, keeps the effort and lets the trust become a formality. What does the reading’s “but trust in God” add that Franklin’s proverb drops?
Day by day deeds better, conduct more beautiful. Giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; and to knowledge temperance.
A person without knowledge and crafts is like a fruitless tree. He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
“I desire distinction for you”, not in wealth but in virtue. Ye are the light of the world: a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.

Every gift can be won by effort, “but guidance is a divine bestowal”. Paul presses that exception hard: it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. If the greatest gift is not earned, what is all the striving for?
Paul also joins the two in one sentence: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God which worketh in you.
The reading quotes this verse: as for those who strive in Us, We surely guide them to Our paths.
“Take hold of the means.” Aesop’s waggoner, stuck in the mud, prays to Hercules and is told to put his own shoulder to the wheel first.
A school needs effort, pure intention and patience. Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Strive with pure intention “and ultimately await the results”. In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper.

“He who is active … will always meet with success.” The Preacher saw otherwise under the sun: the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; time and chance happeneth to them all. The reading concedes this of worldly matters. Why should the Cause be different?

Bahá’u’lláh loved enthusiasm, courage, and finishing what was begun. Roosevelt’s credit goes to the man who is actually in the arena, who strives valiantly and, if he fails, fails while daring greatly.
A pupil understands nothing at first and learns by persisting. Precept upon precept; line upon line; here a little, and there a little.
“How can one increase in faith? You must strive … Search.” Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened.
Capacity must be exercised or it declines. Whosoever hath, to him shall be given; whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath.
“Capacity is in accordance with striving.” Aristotle: we become builders by building and just by doing just acts.
We must strive for the capability to receive grace. God changeth not the condition of a folk until they change that which is in their hearts.
Whatever level is reached, a higher remains. Browning: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for?
Paul near the end of his life: not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after.
In every matter, the utmost effort. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
First consider the hardships, then resolve and set out. Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?

The bird on its branch has a height kings might envy, but, the reading says, without effort or merit. Jesus points to the same birds to opposite purpose: they sow not, neither do they reap, yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Is the bird a warning or a lesson?
Confirmation does not depend on talent; the unimportant make the discoveries. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Ships wrecked and lives lost before the Pole was found. Tennyson’s old Ulysses: to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
“If he does not succeed today he will succeed tomorrow.” Kipling asks for one who can watch the things he gave his life to broken, and stoop and build them up with worn-out tools.
Some are given an iron will and a passion for doing. Brutus: there is a tide in the affairs of men which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
Enthusiasm “is the essential thing”. Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.
“Ceaseless, joyful, ever expanding activity.” Longfellow: let us, then, be up and doing, with a heart for any fate.

Milton, blind in mid-career and unable to work as he had, hears Patience answer him: they also serve who only stand and wait. What place do the readings leave for those who cannot be ceaselessly active?
Humble, active, sincere, zealous: “this is the outcome of life”. Micah’s short list: to do justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly.

“Spread our wings”, the reading says, if we would rise. Isaiah gives wings to those who wait: they that wait upon the Lord shall mount up with wings as eagles. How do waiting and spreading wings go together?
Desire with the heart, humility with the soul, strength with the body, “all your powers”. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

“Effort is needed” to leave the realm of self. Augustine’s prayer, which scandalized Pelagius for seeming to excuse effort: give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt. Who is right about what we are able to do?
Hearts sicken when deprived of striving. I went by the field of the slothful, and, lo, it was all grown over with thorns.
“Man must never get satisfied. He must ever be thirsty.” As the hart panteth after the water brooks.

“There is nothing worse … than satisfaction.” Paul: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. The reading speaks of thirst for the things of God, Paul of want and plenty. Can one be content and never satisfied at once?
“The thirsty one must run after the water.” Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters.
The fountain, the reading says, will not run after the thirsty. In the parable the father sees his son a great way off, and runs. Which picture of God is the truer, or does each correct the other?
Strive for your portion. The Qur’an: man hath only that for which he maketh effort, and his effort will be seen.
God “has called them to striving and seeking”. They which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize; so run, that ye may obtain.
Fix the gaze on lofty stations and strive for them. Forgetting those things which are behind, I press toward the mark.
One must use the means and techniques proper to each field. Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
“The more effort is expended, the more bounty will be received.” Every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour; for we are labourers together with God.
The reading quotes this verse: a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.
The effort is a seed that will yield its harvest. The psalm of the returning exiles: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Some think the goal beyond human effort. Thoreau: if you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; now put the foundations under them.
“Indulge not your bodies with rest.” The Qur’an: so when thou art relieved, still toil, and strive to please thy Lord.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The readings ask for no rest; Jesus offers it. Are these two stages, two temperaments, or a real disagreement?
“Struggle ye, and strive”, since the Beloved was on the field day and night. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
Spend every breath, and be safe from loss. Always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain.
“While there is still oil in thy lamp.” I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
“Let not time slip from thy grasp.” Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
“Time is a cutting sword.” Herrick’s famous counsel draws the opposite moral from the same fact: gather ye rosebuds while ye may. Both urge haste; toward what?
Seize the chance and ignore what yields no fruit. Carlyle: do the duty which lies nearest thee; thy second duty will already have become clearer.

“One must not be idle for a moment day and night.” The psalm calls it vain to rise up early and sit up late, eating the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep. What is the psalmist protecting?
They shall labour ceaselessly and disregard all ease. Paul’s account of his own years: in journeyings often, in perils, in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often.
“Not rest for one moment.” Martha was cumbered about much serving, and it was her sister, sitting still, who was said to have chosen the good part. What does ceaseless activity risk?
In every kind of excellence. Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
“This is the day of the arena.” Hebrews fills the stands: seeing we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
We strive “in gratitude for the favors” of God. What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me?
Whether men reach the higher place “depends upon the efforts which they put forth”. The Buddha: you yourself must make an effort; the Tathagatas are only preachers.
Paul reckons his own effort and then corrects the sum: I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. How would he restate this reading?
What takes years by science and art, the believer does “in a short time” by another power. Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
God loves the highest perfection in every art. Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.
Men should not centre all their efforts on themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.

shortfall: Some forty of the readings (44 to 83) are brief exhortations from letters that say “strive” or “make a mighty effort” with little else; they were given companions where they add an image or a reason (the lamp’s oil, the sword of time, the arena, the harvest, gratitude) and not for each repetition.

philippians-things-of-others.text: Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others
